description_full: Northland Power Inc. operates as a power producer in Canada, the Netherlands, Germany, Colombia, Spain, the United States, and internationally. The company produces electricity from renewable resources, such as offshore and onshore wind; solar; natural gas; and battery energy storage for sale under power purchase agreements and other revenue arrangements. As of December 31, 2025, it owned or had a net economic interest in 3,014 MW of power-producing facilities with a total gross operating capacity of approximately 3,498 MW and a regulated utility. The company was founded in 1987 and is headquartered in Toronto, Canada.

CEO compensation is 2× revenue per employee (modest relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags elevated compensation governance risk (8/10). R&D investment of 3% of revenue (limited) signals commitment to product development and talent.
financial_summary: Northland Power, Inc. is a mid-cap utilities business with a $4.4B market cap on $1.7B of annual revenue.

The top line has compounded at -3% over the past three years, and a shrinking top line is the hardest headwind any business can overcome. Operating margins are contracting by -3.3pp, the first warning that competitive pressure is eroding the franchise.
Returns on capital run at 6% against a 6% cost of capital, which means the business barely earns its keep economically. Gross margins of 90% confirm genuine pricing power.
The business throws off $904M in free cash flow — roughly 53 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders.
On the balance sheet, debt is heavy at 4.1× net debt/EBITDA, and leverage like that is what turns a bad year into a permanent loss, and thin 2.5× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.

Shareholder yield of 4.6% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and within its sector the business captures 1.7× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

Wildfire and climate liability — extreme weather events create catastrophic, uninsurable losses that can push even investment-grade utilities toward restructuring.
